analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee or floor vote; after a September 2019 subcommittee hearing it sat until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the government is barred from negotiating Medicare drug prices with manufacturers. This bill repeals that ban and directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices for the highest-cost Medicare drugs, with a fallback: if talks fail, the price drops to the lowest of several benchmarks, including the average price charged in Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Japan. It would also make drug makers pay rebates for drugs used by low-income Medicare enrollees and let the Secretary set a Medicare drug formulary.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries, who pay Part D premiums and cost-sharing tied to drug prices, and taxpayers, who help fund Medicare's drug benefit. Low-income Medicare enrollees would benefit directly from the new manufacturer rebates.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the 'non-interference' provision that forbids the government from negotiating covered Part D drug prices, and requires the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with manufacturers [S2, S3].

Negotiations are prioritized toward the drugs costing Medicare the most: the 40 highest total expenditures, the 40 with annual spending over $10,000 per beneficiary, the 20 fastest-rising prices, and single-source drugs whose cost exceeds the annual out-of-pocket threshold [S3].
If negotiation fails, the price falls to the lowest of three benchmarks, including the average price available in Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Japan [S3].

Drug manufacturers must pay a rebate for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees whenever Medicare's price exceeds the Medicaid rebate amount, and their drugs can be excluded from coverage entirely if they refuse to sign the rebate agreement [S3].

The Secretary would establish a Medicare drug formulary, or require plans to change theirs, with at least two covered drugs in every therapeutic category, while preserving a process for enrollees to request coverage of drugs not on the formulary [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose pricing power on their biggest-selling Medicare drugs through negotiation, international reference prices, and new low-income rebates. Critics argue some of that cost could come back as reduced investment in developing new medicines.

drawbacks.text: The fallback that uses average prices from five foreign countries, and the Medicaid-style rebates, would cut manufacturers' revenue on their best-selling drugs; the industry's good-faith objection is that this could reduce investment in new drug development [S3].

Shifting formulary design to the Secretary would reduce the flexibility private Part D plans have today to structure their own networks, tiers, and preferred-drug deals, though plans could still negotiate discounts below the negotiated price [S3].
The bill covers only prioritized high-cost drugs, so the majority of lower-priced Part D drugs would remain outside formal negotiation, limiting the savings compared with a broader approach [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the specific drugs that drive most Medicare drug spending, so even a limited negotiation program could produce large savings for beneficiaries and the program. The main honest trade-off is the industry's argument that lower returns on top-selling drugs could slow future drug development; the counterweight is that the negotiation set is limited to a prioritized list of the most expensive drugs rather than everything. On balance, for the people who actually pay Part D premiums, copays, and taxes, the benefits are direct and the costs are diffuse and disputed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, got a subcommittee hearing in September 2019, was never brought up for a committee vote or a floor vote, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Act on January 10, 2019, with 25 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors [S1, S4].
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee [S5].

The Health Subcommittee held a hearing on September 25, 2019; that was the last action on the bill, and no committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept the existing ban on Medicare price negotiation for the rest of that Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 25 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote.

industries.note: Negotiation, the international price fallback, and Medicaid-level rebates for low-income enrollees would cut their revenue on the highest-selling Medicare drugs. Their pricing power over the government's largest drug purchaser is exactly what the bill removes.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: They would buy drugs at negotiated prices, lowering their costs, but the Secretary would gain authority over a formulary or required formulary changes, reducing their control over tiers and preferred-drug deals. The bill does let them negotiate discounts below the negotiated price.
